chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter VIII
paragraphs: Once again Pierre was overtaken by the depression he dreaded so much. For three days after delivering his speech at the lodge, he lay on a sofa at home, seeing no one and going nowhere.
It was just then that he received a letter from his wife, who begged him to see her, telling him how upset she was about him and how she wished to devote her whole life to him.
At the end of the letter she informed him that she would be returning to Petersburg from abroad in a few days.

Shortly after this letter, one of the Masonic Brothers whom Pierre respected less than the others forced his way in to see him. Turning the conversation to Pierre's marriage, he offered some brotherly advice, suggesting that Pierre's harshness toward his wife was wrong and that he was violating one of the fundamental rules of Freemasonry by refusing to forgive the repentant.

At the same time his mother-in-law, Prince Vasili's wife, sent word begging him to come, if only for a few minutes, to discuss an extremely important matter. Pierre could see there was a conspiracy against him and that they wanted to reunite him with his wife, but in his current state of mind, this wasn't even unpleasant to him. Nothing mattered to him. Nothing in life seemed particularly important, and under the weight of the depression that gripped him, he valued neither his freedom nor his determination to punish his wife.
"No one is right and no one is to blame; so she too is not to blame," he thought.

If he didn't immediately agree to a reunion with his wife, it was only because in his depressed state he didn't feel capable of taking any step at all. Had his wife simply come to him, he wouldn't have turned her away. Compared to what was preoccupying him, did it really matter whether he lived with his wife or not?
Without replying to either his wife or his mother-in-law, Pierre set out late one night for Moscow to see Joseph Alexeevich. This is what he wrote in his diary:
Moscow, 17th November

I have just returned from my benefactor and hasten to write down what I experienced. Joseph Alexeevich is living in poverty and has been suffering for three years from a painful bladder disease. No one has ever heard him groan or utter a word of complaint. From morning till late at night, except when he eats his very plain food, he works on his studies. He received me warmly and had me sit on the bed where he lay. I made the sign of the Knights of the East and of Jerusalem, and he responded in kind, asking me with a gentle smile what I had learned and gained in the Prussian and Scottish lodges. I told him everything as best I could, including what I had proposed to our Petersburg lodge, the poor reception I had met with, and my break with the Brothers. Joseph Alexeevich, after remaining silent and thoughtful for a long while, shared his view of the matter, which immediately illuminated my entire past and the future path I should follow. He surprised me by asking whether I remembered the threefold aim of the order: (1) The preservation and study of the mystery. (2) The purification and reformation of oneself for its reception, and (3) The improvement of the human race by striving for such purification. Which is the principal aim of these three? Certainly self-reformation and self-purification. Only toward this aim can we always strive, regardless of circumstances. But at the same time, this very aim demands the greatest efforts from us; and so, led astray by pride, losing sight of this aim, we occupy ourselves either with the mystery — which in our impurity we are unworthy to receive — or seek to reform the human race while ourselves setting an example of baseness and depravity. Illuminism is not a pure doctrine, precisely because it is attracted to social activism and inflated by pride. On these grounds Joseph Alexeevich condemned my speech and my entire course of action, and in the depths of my soul I agreed with him. Speaking of my family affairs he said to me: "The chief duty of a true Mason, as I have told you, lies in perfecting himself. We often think that by removing all the difficulties from our lives we will reach our goal more quickly, but on the contrary, my dear sir, it is only in the midst of worldly cares that we can achieve our three chief aims: (1) Self-knowledge — for man can only know himself through comparison, (2) Self-perfecting, which can only be attained through struggle, and (3) The attainment of the chief virtue — love of death. Only the trials of life can reveal its vanity and nurture our innate love of death, or of rebirth to a new life." These words are all the more remarkable because, despite his great physical suffering, Joseph Alexeevich never tires of life, though he loves death — for which, in spite of the purity and loftiness of his inner being, he does not yet feel himself sufficiently prepared. My benefactor then explained to me in full the meaning of the Great Square of creation and pointed out that the numbers three and seven are the foundation of everything. He advised me not to withdraw from the Petersburg Brothers, but to take only second-rank positions in the lodge, and to try, while steering the Brothers away from pride, to turn them toward the true path of self-knowledge and self-perfecting. Besides this, he advised me personally above all to keep watch over myself, and to that end he gave me a notebook — the one I am now writing in — in which I will henceforth record all my actions.
Petersburg, 23rd November

I am living with my wife again. My mother-in-law came to me in tears and said that Helene was here and begged me to hear her; that she was innocent and miserable at my desertion, and much more. I knew that if I once let myself see her I wouldn't have the strength to keep refusing what she wanted. In my confusion I didn't know whose aid or advice to seek. Had my benefactor been here he would have told me what to do. I went to my room and reread Joseph Alexeevich's letters and recalled my conversations with him, and from all of it concluded that I must not refuse someone who comes asking for help, and must extend a hand to everyone — especially to one so closely bound to me — and that I must bear my cross. But if I forgive her for the sake of doing right, then let our reunion serve only a spiritual purpose. That is what I decided, and what I wrote to Joseph Alexeevich. I told my wife that I asked her to forget the past, to forgive me whatever wrong I may have done her, and that I had nothing to forgive. It gave me joy to tell her this. She need not know how hard it was for me to see her again. I have settled on the upper floor of this big house and am feeling a happy sense of renewal.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter IX
paragraphs: At that time, as always happens, the highest society — the circles that gathered at court and at the grand balls — was divided into several groups, each with its own particular character. The largest of these was the French circle allied with Napoleon, the circle of Count Rumyantsev and Caulaincourt. In this group Helene, as soon as she had settled in Petersburg with her husband, took a very prominent place. She was visited by members of the French embassy and by many people known for their intelligence and polished manners.

Helene had been at Erfurt during the famous meeting of the Emperors and had brought back from there her connections with Napoleonic dignitaries. At Erfurt her success had been brilliant. Napoleon himself had noticed her in the theater and said of her: "That's a superb creature." Her success as a beautiful and elegant woman did not surprise Pierre, for she had become even more attractive than before. What did surprise him was that during these last two years his wife had somehow acquired the reputation of being as charming and witty as she was beautiful. The distinguished Prince de Ligne wrote her eight-page letters. Bilibin saved up his best witticisms to deliver them in Countess Bezukhova's presence. To be received in the Countess Bezukhova's salon was considered a mark of intellectual distinction. Young men read books before attending Helene's evenings so they would have something to say in her salon, and secretaries of the embassy, and even ambassadors, confided diplomatic secrets to her, so that in a way Helene became a force. Pierre, who knew she was very stupid, sometimes attended her evenings and dinner parties — where politics, poetry, and philosophy were discussed — with a strange feeling of bewilderment and dread. At these parties he felt like a conjurer who always expects his trick to be found out. But whether because stupidity was exactly what was needed to run such a salon, or because the people being deceived found pleasure in the deception, the illusion was never exposed, and Helene Bezukhova's reputation as a lovely and clever woman became so firmly established that she could say the emptiest and most foolish things and everybody would go into raptures over every word, finding deep meaning in it that she herself never intended.
* "That's a superb creature."
* (2) "A charming woman, as witty as she is beautiful."

Pierre was exactly the kind of husband a brilliant society woman needed. He was that absent-minded eccentric, a grand nobleman of a husband who was in nobody's way and who, far from lowering the tone of the drawing room, actually enhanced it — his very contrast with his wife making her appear to better advantage. Pierre, during the last two years, as a result of his constant absorption in abstract matters and his genuine indifference to everything else, had acquired in his wife's circle — which held no interest for him — that air of ease, detachment, and goodwill toward all that cannot be faked and therefore commands real respect. He entered his wife's drawing room as one enters a theater: he knew everyone, was equally glad to see everyone, and equally indifferent to them all. Sometimes he joined in a conversation that interested him and, regardless of whether any important diplomats were present, would share his views in his slightly lisping way — views that were sometimes completely at odds with the prevailing tone. But the general opinion of the eccentric husband of "the most distinguished woman in Petersburg" was so well established that no one took his quirks seriously.

Among the many young men who visited the house every day, Boris Drubetskoy — who had already achieved considerable success in the service — was the most intimate friend of the Bezukhov household since Helene's return from Erfurt. Helene called him "my page" and treated him like a child. Her smile for him was the same as for everyone, but sometimes that smile made Pierre uncomfortable. Toward Pierre, Boris behaved with a particularly dignified and mournful deference. This shade of deference also disturbed Pierre. He had suffered so painfully three years before from the humiliation his wife had put him through that he now protected himself from any repeat, first by not being a husband to his wife in any real sense, and second by refusing to allow himself to suspect anything.

"No, now that she's become an intellectual she has finally given up her old infatuations," he told himself. "There has never been a case of a bluestocking having love affairs" — a statement which, though he'd picked it up from somewhere unknown, he believed completely. Yet strangely, Boris's constant presence in his wife's drawing room had a physical effect on Pierre: it made him stiff, constrained, and robbed him of his natural ease of movement.
"What a strange dislike," thought Pierre, "and yet I used to be quite fond of him."

In the eyes of the world Pierre was a great nobleman, the somewhat blind and foolish husband of a distinguished wife, a clever eccentric who did nothing and harmed nobody and was a thoroughly good-natured fellow. But a complex and difficult process of inner transformation was taking place all this time in Pierre's soul, revealing much to him and causing him both spiritual anguish and joy.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter X
paragraphs: Pierre continued with his diary, and this is what he wrote during that time:
24th November

Got up at eight, read the Scriptures, then went to my duties. (On Joseph Alexeevich's advice, Pierre had entered government service and was working on one of the committees.) Came home for dinner and dined alone — the countess had many visitors I don't care for. I ate and drank in moderation and after dinner copied out some passages for the Brothers. In the evening I went down to the countess and told a funny story about B., and only remembered afterwards that I shouldn't have done so when everybody burst out laughing.

I am going to bed with a happy and peaceful mind. Great God, help me to walk in Your ways: (1) to conquer anger through calm and deliberation, (2) to overcome lust through self-discipline and repulsion, (3) to withdraw from worldliness, but not to avoid (a) the service of the state, (b) family duties, (c) relations with friends, and the management of my affairs.
27th November

I got up late. On waking I lay in bed a long time, giving in to laziness. O God, help and strengthen me that I may walk in Your ways! Read the Scriptures, but without proper feeling. Afterward went and paced up and down the large hall. I wanted to meditate, but instead my imagination kept returning to something that happened four years ago, when Dolokhov, meeting me in Moscow after our duel, said he hoped I was enjoying perfect peace of mind despite my wife's absence. At the time I gave him no answer. Now I replayed every detail of that meeting and in my mind gave him the most vicious and bitter replies. I caught myself and drove away that thought only when I realized I was burning with anger — but I did not repent enough. Afterward Boris Drubetskoy came and began telling various stories. His visit irritated me from the start, and I said something unpleasant to him. He responded. I lost my temper and said much that was rude and even cruel to him. He fell silent, and I only came to my senses when it was too late. My God, I simply cannot get along with him. The reason is my own selfishness. I put myself above him and so become much worse than he is, for he is patient with my rudeness while I harbor contempt for him. O God, grant that in his presence I may instead see my own failings, and behave so that he too may benefit. After dinner I fell asleep, and as I was dozing off I clearly heard a voice in my left ear saying: "Your day!"
After this, three pages were left blank in the diary, and then the following was written:

I had a long and instructive conversation alone with Brother V., who advised me to hold fast by Brother A. Though I am unworthy, much was revealed to me. Adonai is the name of the creator of the world. Elohim is the name of the ruler of all. The third name is the unutterable name which means the All. Conversations with Brother V. strengthen, refresh, and support me on the path of virtue. In his presence doubt has no place. The distinction between the shallow teachings of worldly science and our sacred all-embracing teaching is clear to me. Human sciences dissect everything to understand it, and kill everything to examine it. In the holy science of our order all is one, all is known in its completeness and life. The Trinity — the three elements of matter — are sulphur, mercury, and salt. Sulphur is of an oily and fiery nature; in combination with salt, by its fiery nature it arouses a desire in the latter by means of which it attracts mercury, seizes it, holds it, and in combination produces other substances. Mercury is a fluid, volatile, spiritual essence. Christ, the Holy Spirit, Him!...
3rd December

Woke late, read the Scriptures but felt listless. Afterward went and paced up and down the large hall. I wanted to meditate, but instead my imagination kept picturing something that happened four years ago, when Dolokhov ran into me in Moscow after our duel and said he hoped I was enjoying perfect peace of mind despite my wife's absence. At the time I gave him no answer. Now I recalled every detail of that encounter and in my mind gave him the most vicious and bitter replies. I caught myself and pushed the thought away only when I realized I was burning with anger — but I didn't repent enough. Then Boris Drubetskoy came and began telling various stories. His visit irritated me from the start, and I said something unpleasant to him. He responded. I flared up and said much that was rude and even cruel to him. He fell silent, and I came to my senses only when it was too late. My God, I cannot get along with him at all. The cause of this is my own selfishness. I set myself above him and so become much worse than he, for he is patient with my rudeness while I on the contrary harbor contempt for him. O God, grant that in his presence I may see my own failings, and behave so that he too may benefit. After dinner I fell asleep, and as I was dozing off I clearly heard a voice in my left ear saying: "Your day!"

I dreamed I was walking in the dark and was suddenly surrounded by dogs, but I went on without fear. Suddenly a small dog seized my left thigh with its teeth and wouldn't let go. I began to choke it with my hands. No sooner had I torn it off than another, bigger one, began biting me. I lifted it up, but the higher I lifted it the bigger and heavier it grew. Then Brother A. appeared and, taking my arm, led me to a building we could only enter by walking along a narrow plank. I stepped on it, but it bent and gave way and I began to climb a fence I could barely reach with my hands. After much effort I dragged myself up, so that my leg hung down on one side and my body on the other. I looked around and saw Brother A. standing on the fence, pointing me toward a broad avenue and garden, and in the garden was a large and beautiful building. I woke up. O Lord, great Architect of Nature, help me to tear from myself these dogs — my passions, especially the last, which combines in itself the strength of all the others — and help me enter that temple of virtue which I glimpsed in my dream.
7th December

I dreamed that Joseph Alexeevich was sitting in my house, and that I was very glad and wanted to make him welcome. It seemed as if I was chattering endlessly with other people and suddenly remembered that this could not please him, and I wished to go close to him and embrace him. But as soon as I drew near, I saw that his face had changed and grown young, and he was quietly telling me something about the teachings of our order, but so softly that I couldn't hear. Then it seemed we all left the room and something strange happened. We were sitting or lying on the floor. He was telling me something, and I wished to show him my sensitivity, and not listening to what he was saying I began imagining the state of my inner man and the grace of God sanctifying me. Tears came to my eyes, and I was glad he noticed. But he looked at me with annoyance and jumped up, breaking off his remarks. I felt ashamed and asked whether what he'd been saying didn't concern me; but he didn't reply, gave me a kind look, and then we suddenly found ourselves in my bedroom where there is a double bed. He lay down on the edge of it and I burned with longing to be close to him and lie down too. And he said: "Tell me honestly, what is your chief temptation? Do you know it? I think you know it already." Embarrassed by this question, I answered that laziness was my chief temptation. He shook his head in disbelief; and even more ashamed, I said that though I was living with my wife as he had advised, I was not living with her as her husband. To this he replied that one should not deprive a wife of one's embraces, and gave me to understand that that was my duty. But I answered that I would be ashamed to do it, and suddenly everything vanished. I woke up and found in my mind the text from the Gospel: "The life was the light of men. And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not." Joseph Alexeevich's face had looked young and bright. That day I received a letter from my benefactor in which he wrote about "conjugal duties."
9th December

I had a dream from which I awoke with a pounding heart. I saw that I was in Moscow in my house, in the large sitting room, and Joseph Alexeevich came in from the drawing room. I seemed to know at once that the process of spiritual renewal had already taken place in him, and I rushed to meet him. I embraced him and kissed his hands, and he said: "Have you noticed that my face is different?" I looked at him, still holding him in my arms, and saw that his face was young, but that he had no hair on his head and his features were completely changed. And I said: "I would have known you if I'd met you by chance." And I thought to myself: "Am I telling the truth?" And suddenly I saw him lying like a dead body; then he gradually recovered and went with me into my study carrying a large book of drawing paper. I said: "I drew that," and he answered by bowing his head. I opened the book, and on every page there were beautiful drawings. And in my dream I knew that these drawings represented the love adventures of the soul with its beloved. And on the pages I saw a beautiful image of a maiden in transparent garments and with a transparent body, flying up to the clouds. And I seemed to know that this maiden was nothing other than a representation of the Song of Songs. And looking at those drawings I felt that I was doing wrong, but could not tear myself away from them. Lord, help me! My God, if Your forsaking me is Your doing, then Your will be done; but if I am myself the cause, teach me what I should do! I will be destroyed by my depravity if You utterly desert me!

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter XI
paragraphs: The Rostovs' financial situation had not improved during the two years they spent in the country.

Though Nicholas Rostov had stuck firmly to his resolution and was still serving modestly in an undistinguished regiment, spending comparatively little, the way of life at Otradnoe — Mitenka's management of affairs in particular — was such that debts inevitably grew every year. The only obvious course left for the old count was to apply for a government position, so he had come to Petersburg to look for one and also, as he said, to let the girls enjoy themselves one last time.
Soon after their arrival in Petersburg, Berg proposed to Vera and was accepted.

Though in Moscow the Rostovs belonged to the best society without giving it a second thought, in Petersburg their circle of acquaintances was a mixed and uncertain one. In Petersburg they were provincials, and the very people they had entertained in Moscow without asking which set they belonged to now looked down on them.

The Rostovs kept up the same hospitable way of life in Petersburg as in Moscow, and the most varied people gathered at their suppers. Country neighbors from Otradnoe, impoverished old landowners and their daughters, Peronskaya the lady-in-waiting, Pierre Bezukhov, and the son of their district postmaster who had secured a post in Petersburg. Among the men who soon became regular visitors at the Rostovs' house were Boris, Pierre whom the count had met in the street and dragged home with him, and Berg, who spent whole days at the Rostovs' and paid the eldest daughter, Countess Vera, the kind of attention a young man shows when he intends to propose.

Not for nothing had Berg shown everyone his right hand, wounded at Austerlitz, while holding a perfectly unnecessary sword in his left. He told that story so persistently and with such an air of importance that everyone believed in the merit and usefulness of his deed, and he received two decorations for Austerlitz.

In the Finnish war he also managed to distinguish himself. He had picked up a fragment of a grenade that had killed an aide-de-camp near the commander-in-chief and brought it to his superior. Just as after Austerlitz, he told this story at such length and so insistently that everyone believed it had been a necessary thing to do, and he received two more decorations for the Finnish war. By 1809 he was a captain in the Guards, wore medals, and held some special lucrative posts in Petersburg.

Though some skeptics smiled when told of Berg's achievements, it couldn't be denied that he was a conscientious and brave officer, on excellent terms with his superiors, and a moral young man with a brilliant career ahead of him and a secure position in society.

Four years earlier, meeting a German acquaintance in the stalls of a Moscow theater, Berg had pointed out Vera Rostova and said in German: "That girl will be my wife" — and from that moment he had made up his mind to marry her. Now in Petersburg, having assessed the Rostovs' position and his own, he decided the time had come to propose.
* "That girl shall be my wife."

Berg's proposal was at first received with a puzzlement that was not flattering to him. At first it seemed odd that the son of an obscure Baltic gentleman should propose to a Countess Rostova; but Berg's defining quality was such an innocent and good-natured self-regard that the Rostovs gradually came around to thinking it would be a good thing, since he himself was so absolutely convinced that it was good — indeed, excellent. Moreover, the Rostovs' finances were in serious trouble, as the suitor surely knew; and above all, Vera was twenty-four, had been taken out everywhere, and though she was certainly good-looking and sensible, no one had yet proposed to her. So they gave their consent.

"You see," said Berg to a friend — he called this man "friend" only because he knew that everyone has friends — "you see, I've thought it all through, and I wouldn't be marrying if I hadn't considered every angle or if it were in any way a bad match. But on the contrary, my father and mother are now provided for — I've arranged that rental property for them in the Baltic Provinces — and I can live in Petersburg on my pay, and with her fortune and my good management we can get along nicely. I'm not marrying for money — I consider that dishonorable — but a wife should bring her share and a husband his. I have my position in the service, she has connections and some means. In our times that counts for something, doesn't it? But above all, she is a handsome, respectable girl, and she loves me..."
Berg blushed and smiled.

"And I love her, because her character is sensible and very good. Now the other sister, though they're from the same family, is quite different — an unpleasant personality and not the same intelligence. She's so... you know?... Unpleasant... But my fiancee!... Well, you'll be coming," he started to say "to dinner," but changed his mind and said "to take tea with us," and quickly curling his tongue he blew a small round ring of tobacco smoke — a perfect picture of his dream of happiness.

After the initial puzzlement at Berg's proposal, the standard festive mood took over the family, but the celebration was outward and forced. In the family's feelings about this wedding there was an unmistakable awkwardness and unease, as if they were ashamed of not having loved Vera enough and of being so eager to get her off their hands. The old count felt this most keenly. He probably couldn't have said what caused his embarrassment, but it came from the state of his finances. He had no idea how much he had, what his debts amounted to, or what dowry he could give Vera. When his daughters were born he had set aside for each of them an estate with three hundred serfs as a dowry; but one estate had already been sold, and the other was mortgaged with the interest so far in arrears that it would have to be sold too, making it impossible to give it to Vera. Nor did he have any money.

Berg had already been engaged for a month, and only a week remained before the wedding, but the count had still not settled in his own mind the question of the dowry, nor spoken to his wife about it. At one time he thought of giving Vera the Ryazan estate, or selling a forest, at another of borrowing money on a promissory note. A few days before the wedding, Berg came to the count's study early one morning and, with a pleasant smile, respectfully asked his future father-in-law what Vera's dowry would be. The count was so flustered by this long-anticipated question that without thinking he gave the first answer that came to mind: "I appreciate your being businesslike about it... I appreciate it. You'll be satisfied..."

And patting Berg on the shoulder he stood up, hoping to end the conversation. But Berg, smiling pleasantly, explained that if he didn't know for certain how much Vera would have and didn't receive at least part of the dowry in advance, he would have to break off the engagement.
"Because, consider, Count — if I allowed myself to marry without definite means to support my wife, I would be acting dishonorably..."

The conversation ended with the count, who wished to be generous and avoid further pressure, saying that he would give a promissory note for eighty thousand rubles. Berg smiled humbly, kissed the count on the shoulder, and said he was very grateful, but that it was impossible for him to arrange his new life without receiving thirty thousand in cash. "Or at least twenty thousand, Count," he added, "and then a note for only sixty thousand."
"Yes, yes, all right!" said the count hastily. "Only excuse me, my dear fellow, I'll give you twenty thousand and a note for eighty thousand as well. Yes, yes! Kiss me."

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter XII
paragraphs: Natasha was sixteen and it was the year 1809, the very year she had counted to on her fingers with Boris after they had kissed four years ago. Since then she had not seen him. In front of Sonya and her mother, if Boris happened to come up in conversation, she spoke quite freely about that episode as something childish and long-forgotten, hardly worth mentioning. But in the secret depths of her heart, the question of whether her engagement to Boris was a joke or an important, binding promise tormented her.
Since Boris left Moscow in 1805 to join the army, he had not visited the Rostovs. He had been in Moscow several times and had passed near Otradnoe, but had never come to see them.
Sometimes it occurred to Natasha that he didn't want to see her, and this suspicion was confirmed by the sad tone in which her elders spoke of him.
"Old friends are forgotten these days," the countess would say when Boris was mentioned.

Anna Mikhaylovna had also visited them less frequently of late, seemed to carry herself with particular dignity, and always spoke with pride and gratitude about her son's merits and his brilliant career. When the Rostovs came to Petersburg, Boris called on them.

He drove to their house feeling somewhat nervous. The memory of Natasha was his most poetic recollection. But he went with the firm intention of making clear to both her and her parents that the childhood bond between them could not be considered binding on either side. He had a brilliant social position thanks to his closeness to Countess Bezukhova, a brilliant career thanks to the patronage of an important person whose complete confidence he enjoyed, and he was beginning to plan a marriage with one of the richest heiresses in Petersburg — plans that might very easily come to fruition. When he entered the Rostovs' drawing room, Natasha was in her own room. When she heard of his arrival she practically ran into the drawing room, flushed and beaming with a smile far warmer than mere politeness required.

Boris remembered Natasha in a short dress, with dark eyes shining from under her curls and boisterous, childish laughter, as he had known her four years before; and so he was taken aback when a quite different Natasha entered. His face showed delighted astonishment. This expression pleased Natasha.
"Well, do you recognize your little madcap playmate?" asked the countess.
Boris kissed Natasha's hand and said he was amazed at the change in her.
"How pretty you've become!"
"I should think so!" replied Natasha's laughing eyes.
"And is Papa older?" she asked.

Natasha sat down and, without joining in Boris's conversation with the countess, silently and carefully studied her childhood sweetheart. He felt the weight of that determined and affectionate gaze and glanced at her from time to time.

Boris's uniform, spurs, cravat, and the way his hair was styled were all impeccable and in the latest fashion. This Natasha noticed at once. He sat somewhat sideways in the armchair next to the countess, adjusting with his right hand the spotless glove that fit his left hand like a second skin, and he spoke with a particularly refined pursing of his lips about the entertainments of the highest Petersburg society, recalling with gentle irony their old times in Moscow and Moscow acquaintances. It was no accident, Natasha sensed, that when speaking of the highest aristocracy he mentioned an ambassador's ball he had attended, and invitations he had received from such-and-such dignitaries.

All this time Natasha sat silent, looking up at him from under her brows. This gaze disturbed and confused Boris more and more. He looked toward her more frequently, losing the thread of what he was saying. He stayed no more than ten minutes, then rose and took his leave. Those same curious, challenging, somewhat mocking eyes still followed him. After his first visit Boris told himself that Natasha attracted him just as much as ever, but that he must not give in to that feeling, because marrying her — a girl with almost no fortune — would mean the ruin of his career, while renewing their old intimacy without intending to marry her would be dishonorable. Boris made up his mind to avoid meeting Natasha, but despite that resolution he called again a few days later and began calling often and spending whole days at the Rostovs'. It seemed to him that he ought to have a frank talk with Natasha, tell her that the old days must be forgotten, that despite everything she could not be his wife, that he had no means, and they would never let her marry him. But he couldn't bring himself to do it and felt awkward about broaching the subject. Day by day he became more entangled. It seemed to her mother and Sonya that Natasha was in love with Boris as of old. She sang him his favorite songs, showed him her album, made him write in it, would not let him mention the past — making it clear how delightful the present was — and every day he left in a daze, without having said what he'd meant to say, not knowing what he was doing or why he came or how it would all end. He stopped visiting Helene and received reproachful notes from her every day, yet he continued spending whole days at the Rostovs'.
